notes.meaning: God spoke the Ten Commandments aloud from Mount Sinai with great power and majesty. He had already written this moral law on human hearts from the beginning, but now He gave it in spoken words so everyone would know it clearly. His voice revealed His holy nature and showed His people how He called them to live.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that these commandments are direct, absolute commands without stated penalties, a pattern that is rare in ancient legal codes.

notes.meaning: God introduces Himself as the Lord who rescued Israel out of cruel slavery in Egypt. Because He created them and redeemed them, He possesses full authority to tell them how to live. He reminds them of His goodness first so they will obey Him out of love and gratitude.

The first commandment teaches that the Lord alone must be worshipped. Israel was forbidden to turn to false gods or to place any created thing alongside the true Creator. Nothing in our lives should ever be loved, feared, or trusted more than God Himself.

differ.view: Counts this verse as the first commandment, keeping the rule against idols separate as the second commandment.
Combines this verse with the prohibition against idols into a single first commandment.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Combines the command to have no other gods with the ban on making images into one first commandment, following the ancient numbering of Augustine.

notes.meaning: God forbids making any statue, carving, or picture of anything in creation to use as an object of worship. Because God is an invisible Spirit, no physical shape can ever represent Him. Trying to picture God with human hands diminishes His majesty and leads people into false worship.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Distinguishes between worshipping false idols and honoring religious statues or icons of God, angels, and saints, teaching that the commandment only forbids worshipping creatures as gods.

notes.meaning: God will not share His praise with idols, just as a loving husband will not share his wife's devotion with another. Those who hate God and continue in their parents' rebellion bring painful consequences onto their families for generations. Yet God is far more eager to show mercy than to punish, pouring out His steadfast love to thousands of generations of those who love and obey Him.

differ.view: Views the passing down of fathers' sins to children not as an inescapable curse, but as children repeating the rebellious sins of their parents against God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Teaches that ongoing problems such as poverty, illness, or repeated failures can be caused by inherited generational curses or family spirits that need to be broken.

notes.meaning: God commands His people to treat His holy name with the deepest reverence. His name represents who He is, so it must never be used in false oaths, flippant conversation, or insincere prayers. The Lord warns that He will hold everyone accountable who uses His name in a careless or disrespectful way.

God tells Israel to remember the Sabbath and keep it set apart for Him. The word remember shows that this day of rest was already known from the beginning of creation. God's people set this day aside to rest from their daily labor and focus on worshipping Him.

differ.view: Believes the moral requirement to keep one day in seven holy continues today as the Christian Sabbath, which moved from Saturday to Sunday after Christ's resurrection.
Many hold that the fourth commandment as a covenant law was fulfilled in Christ and is not legally binding on Christians, though taking a weekly day of rest remains wise and good.
Teaches that the universal principle of taking a holy day of rest after six days of work remains in effect on Sunday, the Christian memorial of Christ's resurrection.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Numbers this as the third commandment, interpreting it as an obligation to keep the Lord's Day holy by attending Mass and resting from unnecessary work.

notes.meaning: God provides six days for regular work, but the seventh day is reserved as a holy rest belonging to Him. This rest covers everyone in the community, including children, servants, visiting foreigners, and work animals. Masters were forbidden to make others work while they rested, ensuring that everyone received relief from daily toil.

The pattern for the Sabbath is rooted in the creation of the world. The Lord made the heavens and the earth in six days and rested on the seventh, taking pleasure in His finished work. Because He blessed the seventh day and made it holy, His people are invited to enter that same rest with Him.

Children are commanded to show honor, respect, and obedience to both their father and mother. Parents serve as God's appointed guides to nurture and teach their households. God attaches a special promise of a long and prosperous life in the land to encourage faithful, caring obedience to parents.

God protects human life by forbidding the unjust killing of any person. Human beings are created in God's image, making every person's life precious in His eyes. This command also forbids inward hatred, malicious anger, and harmful desires against others.

This command protects marriage by forbidding unfaithfulness between husbands and wives. God calls both men and women to live pure and modest lives in what they do and say. It also forbids lustful looks and improper desires that begin secretly in the heart.

God protects each person's rightful property and goods by commanding everyone not to steal. This rule forbids robbery, dishonest business deals, cheating, and keeping back wages that belong to workers. Instead of taking what belongs to others, believers are called to work honestly and protect their neighbor's well-being.

This commandment guards the truth and protects our neighbor's good reputation. It forbids lying in court, spreading gossip, making false accusations, or twisting someone's words to do them harm. God calls His people to be truthful in all things and to defend the character of others.

The tenth commandment reaches deep into the heart by forbidding coveting, which is an unlawful craving for what belongs to someone else. Wanting another person's home, spouse, or property comes from being discontent with what God has given us. Cultivating a thankful heart protects us from being pulled into other sins against our neighbors.

differ.view: Divides this verse into two separate commandments, making the desire for a neighbor's house the ninth commandment and the desire for his wife or goods the tenth.
Maintains that this verse forms a single commandment against all forms of coveting, treating it as the tenth commandment.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Divides this verse into the ninth commandment against desiring another person's spouse and the tenth commandment against desiring another person's property.

notes.meaning: The Israelites heard the sound of thunder and trumpet blasts, and they watched lightning flash across the smoke-covered mountain. These frightening sights and sounds displayed the supreme power and majesty of God as He gave His holy law. Overcome with deep awe and fear, the people backed away and stood at a distance.

Terrified by the roaring mountain, the people begged Moses to speak to them instead of God. They recognized that frail and sinful humans could not bear the direct, thunderous voice of the holy Lord without dying. Their plea showed that people need a mediator to stand between a holy God and sinful humanity.

Moses told the trembling people not to be paralyzed by terror. God did not send the fire and thunder to destroy them, but to test their loyalty and place a healthy, reverent awe in their hearts. Having a holy respect for God's power would keep them from turning aside into sin.

The people stayed back in fear while Moses walked forward into the thick darkness where God's presence dwelt. Moses did not dare to go on his own strength, but God called him and brought him near by grace. In this way, Moses pointed forward to Christ, the great Go-Between who brings us near to God.

The Lord instructed Moses to remind the people that they had heard His voice speaking directly from heaven. Because God had revealed His will to them in clear words, they did not need to guess what He was like. Hearing the true God from heaven was all the proof they needed of His reality and power.

God commanded the people never to make idols out of silver or gold to stand alongside Him or represent Him. Since they saw no physical form when God spoke from the mountain, making statues would only corrupt their view of Him. Any attempt to picture the spiritual God in metal leads straight to idolatry.

God told Israel to build simple altars out of soil or turf for offering their animal sacrifices. These sacrifices were gifts brought to make atonement, which means making peace with God and covering their guilt. The Lord promised that in every place where He chose to reveal His name, He would come down and bless them.

If Israel made an altar of stone, they were forbidden from cutting or shaping the stones with iron tools. Chiseling the stones into fancy shapes could tempt the people to carve images and slide into idolatrous habits. God wanted their attention placed fully on Him and the sacrifice, not on the human skill used to build the altar.

God commanded that His altars should not have steps leading up to them, so that the priests would not be uncovered while serving. Because priests wore long, flowing garments, climbing stairs could lead to an accidental loss of modesty before the altar. God requires purity, decency, and reverence whenever His people approach Him in worship.
